blocks.text: Provide one interface for creating a family of related objects, so a client can never mix products from different families.

An **abstract factory** declares one creation method per product kind. Each **concrete factory** returns a matching set: everything from the same vendor, platform or environment. The client receives the factory once and asks it for every product it needs.

items: **Varies:** the whole family, swapped by changing one factory.
**Cost:** adding a new product kind changes every factory.

blocks.text: The point is consistency across products. If you create only one kind of object, you want a Factory Method, not this.

walkthrough.note: Two abstract products. Each is a functional interface here, so implementations can be lambdas while the type stays distinct.
The abstract factory: one method per product kind. This interface is the only thing the client ever depends on.
A concrete factory for development. Both products it returns belong to the local family and reference each other's conventions.
A second family with state of its own, the bucket name. Swapping `Infra` swaps blob storage and messaging together.
`Uploader` asks one factory for both products. It cannot pair S3 storage with an in-memory bus, because it never names a concrete product.
The environment picks a factory once, at the edge. The rest of the program is identical in both runs.

blocks.text: A checkout that supports several payment providers.

Each provider needs a matching trio: a `PaymentGateway`, a `WebhookVerifier` and a `ReceiptFormatter`. A Stripe webhook signature is meaningless to an Adyen verifier, so mixing them is a production incident. A `PaymentKit` factory hands out all three from the same provider, and the region configuration selects one kit per tenant.
Payoff: onboarding a provider is one new kit, and incompatible combinations cannot be written.

lists.title: Use when
items: Products must be used together and come from one vendor, platform or environment.
You swap an entire stack, such as local versus cloud, with one decision.
Clients should be unable to mix incompatible products.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Only one product kind varies; a Factory Method or a `Supplier` is lighter.
New product kinds appear often, since each one edits every factory.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Product kinds that differ in capability force lowest-common-denominator interfaces.
Leaking a concrete product type to the client re-introduces the coupling.
Forgetting that every new family must implement all methods.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A factory interface whose products have no relationship to each other.
Factory-of-factories chains with one implementation each.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Dependency injection containers pick the family through configuration, replacing hand-written selection.
A record of suppliers can stand in for a factory interface of two or three products.

rows.difference: Each abstract-factory method is usually implemented as a factory method. The difference is scope: Factory Method defers one creation, Abstract Factory guarantees a coherent family.
Builder constructs one complex product step by step and hands it back at the end. Abstract Factory returns several simple products immediately, each on request.
A concrete factory can hold prototypes and clone them instead of calling constructors, so a family is configured rather than subclassed.
A concrete factory is usually stateless or shared, so it is often held as one instance per application or container.
A container can wire a whole family from configuration. Abstract Factory is the explicit, code-level version of the same decision.

options.why: One interface creates several related products, and each implementation returns a consistent matching set.
That would be one overridable creation step inside an algorithm; here three product kinds are produced as a family.
Nothing is assembled step by step into one object; each method returns a separate finished product.
The methods create objects rather than encapsulate an algorithm the caller runs.

exercises.scenario: A reporting tool must run against either a PostgreSQL or an Oracle stack. Each stack needs its own query dialect, connection pool and migration runner, and mixing a Postgres dialect with an Oracle pool is a known source of bugs.

options.why: Several related products must come from the same family, and the choice of stack is made once.
It creates one product at a time and cannot enforce that the dialect, pool and runner match.
The problem is not assembling one complex object but keeping several separate objects compatible.
Adapters translate an existing interface; they do not guarantee that created objects belong together.

exercises.prompt: Explain Abstract Factory in your own words: what does it guarantee, and what does it make expensive?

modelAnswer.text: An abstract factory has one creation method per product kind, and each concrete factory returns a matching family. The client holds only the factory, so it cannot mix products from different families. The price is rigidity: a new product kind means changing every factory.

keyPoints: One factory interface, one method per product kind
Concrete factories return a consistent family
The client depends only on abstractions and cannot mix families
Adding a product kind edits every factory
Single product variation calls for Factory Method instead
